conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to check in on how moms are feeling after their baby arrives. The tool we’ll use today is called the EPDS, a brief questionnaire that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up any time in the first year postpartum.

Anything you share stays between you and our care team; there’s no judgment here—only support. I’ll ask ten short questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience. When you’re ready, we can dive in.

First question: In the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things or take pleasure in the little moments of life, even if it’s just a hot cup of coffee or a quick smile from your baby?

Honestly… I do still enjoy some things, but it’s like the joy is turned way down. When my baby looks up at me and smiles, it still melts my heart, but the feeling fades faster than it used to. Even that first hot sip of coffee—used to feel like a tiny celebration, and now it’s just… coffee. I can’t tell if I’m too tired to feel it or if the sparkle is just gone.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband made that goofy face while changing a diaper—but it takes way more effort than before. Most days I feel too worn out to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now even those feel like chores I have to push myself through. I’ll mark “no, not much.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his stomach, or that I wasn’t soothing him the “right” way. Rationally I know babies just have rough days, but I still catch myself wondering what I did wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like last night, I kept checking that he was breathing every few minutes even though the monitor was on. Nothing specific triggered it—I just couldn’t shake the tight feeling in my chest.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like this low-level scared feeling that something might go wrong with the baby. It’s not full-on panic, but it’s enough to make my stomach knot up out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes... most days. Between the feedings, the laundry, and trying to grab a shower, it feels like I'm always one step behind. Yesterday I just sat on the nursery floor and cried for a minute because I couldn't figure out what to tackle next.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t call it “so unhappy,” but I do lie there with my mind racing—mostly about whether the baby’s okay or if I’ll hear him cry. I end up staring at the ceiling for an hour or more a few nights a week, even when I’m exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad at times—like a heaviness settles in—but it’s not every moment. It comes in waves, usually when I’m alone during a late-night feeding. I wouldn’t say miserable, but definitely down more days than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice when I felt overwhelmed, but actual crying—like full-on sobbing—hasn’t happened. Mostly I just feel kind of flat or tired instead of teary.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired and stretched thin, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia: markedly reduced enjoyment/anticipation (Q2); laughter requires effort (Q1)  
- Low mood: intermittent sadness, “heaviness,” flat affect (Q8)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety: nocturnal hyper-vigilance, chest tightness, fear of harm to infant (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “one step behind,” tearful when alone (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to racing thoughts about infant safety (Q7)  

Frequency / severity  
- Symptoms present “more days than not,” interfere with daily functioning; no frank panic attacks, no suicidal ideation (Q10 denied).  

Screening significance  
Pattern consistent with possible mild–moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; meets threshold for further assessment (EPDS items suggest score range 10–12). No acute safety concerns at this time.  

Risk factors noted  
- Primiparity, sleep disruption, self-criticism, anxiety focused on infant well-being.  

Recommendation  
Continue to formal assessment (EPDS total score, PHQ-9/GAD-7) and consider referral for perinatal mental health evaluation.
